item.text: I’m checking the actual analysis rule against randomized assignment, especially what the reported censoring means for this HbA1c result and whether the sources identify an inappropriate exclusion.

### Signalling question 2.6 — Appropriate analysis

**Answer: probably_yes.** The paper says that all 291 randomized participants were included in the intention-to-treat population and reports 144 and 147 in the randomized groups ([main article, p. 3, lines 89–93, 119–120](#); [p. 4, lines 1–2)). For efficacy, it censored data from the start of rescue therapy or premature study-drug discontinuation, then used a mixed-model repeated-measures analysis ([p. 3, lines 91–100]). The figure caption confirms that this rule applied to the reported analyses ([p. 5, lines 1–7]).

This supports an analysis organized by randomized assignment. The censoring rule creates uncertainty about how participants with post-randomization events contributed to the Week 28 estimate: the report does not give the primary outcome’s analyzed counts or explain the model’s handling of observations after censoring. The trial reports one rescue-therapy case, in the dulaglutide group ([p. 7, lines 7–9]). It also reports study discontinuations, but does not establish which participants lacked HbA1c measurements or whether any observed HbA1c values were omitted ([p. 4, lines 1–3]; visual extraction, p. 4, lines 1–5). Completion counts alone cannot resolve that.

The registry lists 133 and 142 participants for the outcome analysis, defined as randomized participants with baseline and at least one post-baseline HbA1c measurement ([registry, p. 1, lines 1898–1920]). That is consistent with an available-measurement analysis, but it does not establish whether the article’s Week 28 estimate used that same population or how the censoring rule affected it. The supplement’s 139/147 counts and last-observation-carried-forward rule concern secondary composite endpoints, so they do not clarify the primary continuous HbA1c analysis ([supplement, p. 2, lines 1–2, 43–47]). Given the explicit all-randomized population and no source evidence of an adherence-restricted or wrong-group analysis, probable yes is supported; the censoring and population details prevent a firmer yes.

### Signalling question 2.7 — Potential substantial impact

**Not activated.** With 2.6 answered probably_yes, this conditional question does not apply.
